title: A raffle for the top k
allegory: Top-k sampling is a raffle behind a velvet rope: every word holds tickets in proportion to its probability, only the k words holding the most tickets get past the rope, and one ticket is drawn from those alone.
map: every word the model could say, each holding raffle tickets
the vocabulary with its next-token probabilities
only the k biggest ticket-holders get past the rope
keep the top-k logits and treat the rest as −inf
recounting the tickets among those left
renormalising over the survivors, ratios unchanged
drawing one ticket from the drum
always handing the prize to the favourite
greedy or beam-search decoding: bland, repetitive text

cap.1: A model that predicts words well can still write awful stories. Always choosing its single favourite word gives safe, common, repetitive text.
cap.2: Fan, Lewis and Dauphin found beam search, which hunts for the most likely continuation, gave bland, repetitive stories. The model was fine; the way they read words out of it was the problem.
cap.3: Fan et al. (ACL 2018): in open-ended story generation, beam search yielded overly common, repetitive text. Decoding is a design choice layered on the same logits, not a detail.

cap.1: So run a raffle. Only the ten words holding the most tickets get past the velvet rope. Then draw one ticket from those ten. The rest go home.
cap.2: Top-k sampling: keep the k most likely tokens, renormalise their probabilities to sum to 1, sample one. Fan et al. used k = 10. The long tail of unlikely words never gets a chance.
cap.3: Truncate the next-token distribution to its k largest entries, renormalise over the survivors, sample. It survives as the top_k parameter in most text-generation APIs.

chapters.name: Cut, then recount
chapters.title: GPT-2 after 'John and Mary went to the', top_k = 5

cap.1: Real GPT-2 numbers after 'John and Mary went to the': the top five words hold about 14% of the tickets. Cut the rest, recount, and church wins nearly half.
cap.2: Top-5 keeps ' church' 0.0648, ' house' 0.0367, ' temple' 0.0145, ' same' 0.0104, ' Church' 0.0097. Renormalised over those five, church gets about 0.48. ARENA checks your sampler against exactly these.
cap.3: Renormalising divides by the survivors' mass (≈ 0.136), so their ratios are preserved. Over 10,000 samples your empirical frequencies should match the renormalised reference within sampling noise.

cap.1: In code it's about four lines: find the top k scores, hand them straight to the raffle drum, then look up which real word the winning ticket belongs to.
cap.2: torch.topk(logits, k) gives values and indices; Categorical(logits=values).sample() draws one; map it back through the indices. No softmax, no renormalising by hand.
cap.3: Stay in log-space: Categorical normalises unnormalised logits itself, so exponentiating and renormalising by hand is redundant and loses precision. Order: frequency penalty, temperature, top-k.

chapters.name: Two knobs, one trap
chapters.verdict: Temperature never changes who gets past the rope, only how the tickets are shared.

cap.1: Turning the temperature down never changes who gets past the rope, only how the tickets are shared. Do both at once and the favourite hogs the drum: loops.
cap.2: Dividing logits by T keeps their order, so the top-k set is the same at any temperature. Low T plus truncation hands nearly all the mass to one token, and output loops. Pick one knob.
cap.3: T is monotone, so it can't change top-k membership, only the mass within it: k and T compound. A frequency penalty does reorder logits, so it can break loops. Argmax mass above ~0.9 means greedy.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: The sampler picks the word, not the model
top_k sits in nearly every generation API
top-p moves the rope with confidence

cap.1: When you run evals or generate data, these knobs shape what you see. Same model, different sampler, different behaviour.
cap.2: You'll set top_k and temperature in almost every generation call you make. Top-p refines the idea: it keeps a fixed amount of probability rather than a fixed number of words.
cap.3: To understand or steer behaviour, separate the model's distribution from the decoder's choices: a result at top_k = 10, T = 1 is a claim about the model plus its sampler.

readouts.label: verdict
readouts.f: softmax([3, 1.5, 1.2, 0.5, 0.3, 0, -0.5, -1].map((v, i) => i < k ? v/T : -1e9))[0] > 0.9 ? 'effectively greedy: expect loops' : 'still a real raffle'

caption.1: Set k to 8, then drag the temperature down. All eight words stay in the drum, yet the favourite ends up with nearly every ticket. Then try T = 1 with a small k.
caption.2: Temperature never changes which words survive the cut, only how tickets are shared. Watch effective choices: low T shrinks it towards 1 even with k = 8. Past 90% for the favourite, you're decoding greedily.
caption.3: Effective choices = exp(entropy) of the truncated, tempered distribution. k bounds the support; T sets concentration within it. At k = 8, T = 0.3 the favourite holds 99%: wide support, one real option.

where_else: Top-p (nucleus) sampling: keep a fixed probability mass, so the cut moves with the model's confidence
Beam search, which keeps k whole sequences alive instead of k tokens at one step
The temperature, top_k and frequency-penalty knobs on nearly every LLM API call

hamming.what: A way to turn next-token probabilities into a choice: keep the k likeliest tokens, renormalise, and draw one at random.
hamming.when: Whenever you generate open-ended text and want variety without letting the long tail of unlikely words in.
hamming.why: Always taking the likeliest word gives bland, repetitive text and sampling from everything lets nonsense in; truncating and then sampling is the cheap middle.

object.title: The velvet-rope raffle
object.subtitle: Front row: every word's share of tickets. Back row: the same words after the rope and a recount.

cap.1: Front row: every word's share of the tickets. Back row: after only the top three get past the rope and the tickets are recounted.
cap.2: Row 1 is softmax over all logits; row 2 keeps the top 3 and renormalises, so the survivors grow in proportion.
cap.3: Truncation zeroes the tail and rescales the survivors by 1/(their total mass), preserving ratios within the set.

cap.1: Let all eight through and the two rows match. Top-k with k as big as the vocabulary is just plain sampling.
cap.2: With k equal to the vocabulary size nothing is cut, so top-k reduces to ordinary sampling.
cap.3: k = |V| is the identity truncation: the renormalising constant is 1.

cap.1: Cool the temperature. The same three words still get through, but now the favourite towers over the other two.
cap.2: Lower T sharpens the distribution without changing the ranking, so the survivors are the same and the top one dominates.
cap.3: Logits/T is monotone in each logit, so argsort and the top-k set are invariant; only within-set entropy falls.

cap.1: k = 1: one word gets every ticket. That is greedy decoding, the boring favourite from the start of the film.
cap.2: With k = 1 the sampler always returns the argmax: greedy decoding.
cap.3: Top-1 sampling is deterministic argmax decoding, which is prone to repetition in open-ended generation.

cap.1: Warm it up with k = 5. The five survivors share the tickets more evenly, and the rope still keeps the tail out.
cap.2: Higher T flattens the shares among the survivors while truncation still excludes the unlikely tail.
cap.3: High T raises entropy within the support; truncation bounds the support, so the tail's nonsense stays excluded.

predict.q: You lower the temperature. Does the set of top-k words change?

options.t: No: the ranking is kept, so the same words survive

predict.why: Dividing logits by T keeps their order; only the shares inside the set change.

predict.q: What is top-k sampling with k = 1?

options.t: Greedy decoding: always the likeliest word

predict.why: One survivor gets all of the renormalised mass.

predict.q: Why hand the top-k logits straight to Categorical instead of softmaxing first?

options.t: Categorical normalises logits itself; doing it by hand only loses precision

predict.why: Stay in log-space: Categorical(logits=...) does the normalising for you.

object.where: Any shortlist cut before a weighted draw: top-p sampling, and beam search, which keeps k whole sequences instead of k tokens.
